_comment: Language-neutral admission vectors for CheckCanonicalizable / Canonicalize in the shared ld-data-integrity library. HAND-MAINTAINED and intended to be shared with the TypeScript implementation: the Go tests read it, and a port that reads the same file is what would force the two implementations to agree. accept[]: the check returns no error. refuse[]: the check returns an admission error; 'rule' is the rule id and 'path' the RFC 6901 JSON Pointer it reports. 'rule': null means the document violates several rules at once and the order among rules is unspecified, so only refusal is asserted. 'rule' set with 'path': null means one rule is violated at several locations and which location is reported is unspecified. Object members are visited in Unicode code point order of their keys (the same as UTF-8 byte order, which Go's sort.Strings gives; NOT UTF-16 code unit order, which JavaScript's default Array.prototype.sort gives), so among sibling keys breaking the same rule the one first in code point order is reported; the 'key order' vector is the case where the two orders disagree. A document's value count includes the root and every object, array and scalar (null included), @context's array and strings included; object keys are not values. A document's byte count is the total UTF-8 byte length of every string value plus every object key, at any depth, @context included (its own 8-byte key and each of its strings count like any other member); numbers, booleans and null contribute nothing, and JSON quoting or escaping is not counted. generated.accept[] and generated.refuse[] hold the byte-budget vectors as templates, because each expands to about 128 KiB. Expand 'doc' recursively by these rules and no others. (1) An object that has a "$repeat" key must have exactly the two keys "$repeat" and "$times", where the value of "$repeat" is a string s (itself not expanded) and the value of "$times" is a non-negative integer n (a JSON number with no fractional part); it becomes the string s repeated n times. (2) An object that has an "$object" key must have exactly that one key, whose value is an array of two-element arrays [k, v]; it becomes an object with one member per pair, whose key is k expanded (which must yield a string) and whose value is v expanded; no two pairs may yield the same key. (3) Any other object is literal: none of its keys may begin with "$", and each member value is expanded in place. (4) Array elements are expanded in place; strings, numbers, booleans and null are left unchanged. Anything outside these rules is a fixture error that must fail the test run, never be read as a literal object: an object with a "$repeat" or "$object" key not of the exact form above, a literal key beginning with "$", an $object pair that is not a two-element array, a k that does not yield a string, or two pairs yielding the same key. Because rule (3) is applied only to objects written in the file, a key produced by $object may begin with "$". 'bytes' is the expanded document's byte count, which each test must verify before using the vector; the expanded vectors are then checked exactly like accept[] and refuse[]. dataset.accept[] and dataset.refuse[] hold vectors for the dataset-level rules, which Canonicalize applies to the RDF dataset a document expands to, after the rules above and before canonicalizing; CheckCanonicalizable does not apply them, so every dataset vector must pass it. Dataset vectors are processed with a document loader that resolves the library's vendored contexts plus every entry of dataset.contexts, which maps a context URL to the file holding it, as a path relative to the directory of this file. dataset.accept[]: Canonicalize returns no error, and its output is byte-identical to a plain URDNA2015 normalization of the same document to application/n-quads with the same loader. dataset.refuse[]: Canonicalize returns an admission error whose 'rule' is given and whose 'path' is always the empty string, because these rules refuse a document as a whole; 'rule' and 'path' are never null here. The two lists are paired by index: dataset.accept[i] is the counterpart of dataset.refuse[i], a document of the same shape changed only as far as it must be to clear the rule dataset.refuse[i] breaks, and breaking no dataset rule itself. Canonicalize applies the dataset rules in this order and reports the first one a document breaks: 'blank-node-budget', then 'output-budget', then 'indistinguishable-blank-nodes'. Rule 'blank-node-budget': the dataset holds more than 1024 distinct blank nodes. It has no vectors here; its boundary documents are built by each language's tests. Rule 'output-budget': the dataset's estimated canonical output is more than 131072 bytes (128 KiB); an estimate of exactly 131072 is admitted. The budget is set this low because the reference canonicalizer assembles its output by repeated string concatenation, appending each statement to the output built so far, so what one call allocates grows with the output length times the statement count. The estimate is defined identically in both languages, and the two compute the same number whenever their canonical outputs agree, which the shared vectors are chosen to ensure. Let n be the number of distinct blank nodes in the dataset and, when n is at least 1, let W be 6 (the length of _:c14n) plus the number of decimal digits of n-1, the length of the longest of the canonical labels _:c14n0 to _:c14n(n-1). For each quad, take its N-Quad line as the library's serializer writes it (json-gold's toNQuad in Go, rdf-canonize's NQuads.serializeQuad in TypeScript) with the blank-node labels ToRDF gave it, subtract the length of each blank-node label occurring in the subject, object or graph position, and add W for each such occurrence. The estimate is the sum over all quads, and is never less than the length of the canonical output. A document is refused under this rule without the rest of its dataset being serialized once the running sum is over the budget. The simplest case is one node with a long IRI that is the subject of many statements: the output repeats the IRI once per statement while the JSON carries it once. Two pairs hold that shape. In the first, the accept counterpart is the same shape with fewer statements. The second is the boundary: the refuse vector is estimated at 131073 bytes, and its accept counterpart is the same document with its first literal one byte shorter, estimated at exactly 131072. Each vector's name states its exact estimate as '(estimate N bytes)'. Boundary documents of other shapes, with blank nodes, named graphs or multi-byte text, are built by each language's tests. Rule 'indistinguishable-blank-nodes': the dataset holds two blank nodes with the same first-degree hash (RDFC-1.0 Hash First Degree Quads), that is, the same sorted list of the quads mentioning each in any position, serialized with that node written _:a and every other blank node _:z; two identical entries of an array of objects are the simplest case. Its accept counterparts are its refuse vectors with the repeated entries made distinct. Both implementations also refuse, under rule 'ill-formed-string', any object key or string value that is not well-formed Unicode, at the RFC 6901 pointer of the offending member or value. A key's bytes are counted first, then it is judged well-formed, and only then are reserved-key, compact-iri-key and context-shape applied to it; a string value's bytes are counted first, then it is judged well-formed, then 'tab-character' is applied to it, and only then 'blank-node-label'. TypeScript observes such a string as a lone surrogate, which JSON.parse keeps; Go observes one only as invalid UTF-8 in a document built in code, because encoding/json replaces both a lone surrogate and invalid UTF-8 with U+FFFD while decoding. No JSON text can therefore carry one to both languages, so those vectors live in each language's tests rather than here. Rule 'depth-budget': the root object or array is at depth 1, each object or array nested in another is one deeper than it, and strings, numbers, booleans and null add no depth. A document is refused when any object or array is at a depth greater than 32, at the RFC 6901 pointer of the first object or array at depth 33 in walk order (object members in code point order of their keys, array elements in index order); the walk does not enter that object or array, so nothing inside it is judged. The depth is judged as the walk enters an object or array, after that object or array has been counted against the value budget, so a document whose first object or array at depth 33 is also its 1025th value is refused under 'value-budget'. Everything the walk visits before it is judged by the other rules as usual: a member's key is counted, judged well-formed and checked by the key rules before the walk enters the member's value, and an @context value is refused under 'context-shape' before its contents are walked. Rule 'tab-character': a string value containing U+0009 (TAB), at any depth and @context strings included, is refused at the RFC 6901 pointer of that value. Object keys are not checked by this rule: a key becomes an IRI only through a term its context defines, and no shipped context defines a term containing a TAB, so a key's TAB never reaches the canonical output. The rule exists because the two N-Quads serializers escape literals differently: json-gold escapes backslash, double quote, LF, CR and TAB, rdf-canonize only backslash, double quote, LF and CR, so of the characters a literal can hold TAB is the one whose canonical bytes differ between the implementations. Expected output: an accept vector may carry its expected canonical N-Quads, which is the same for every implementation and is compared byte for byte with what Canonicalize returns under every loader of the tests that resolves the document's contexts (the vendored contexts alone, and the vendored contexts plus dataset.contexts). When the output is at most 4096 bytes of UTF-8, 'nquads' holds it exactly; otherwise 'nquads_sha256' holds the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of its UTF-8 bytes and 'nquads_length' its length in bytes. A vector carries one form or the other, never both. Every dataset.accept[] vector carries an expected output. Every accept[] and generated.accept[] vector that either implementation's canonicalizer processes under the vendored contexts plus dataset.contexts carries either an expected output or 'known_divergence', and no other vector carries either. 'known_divergence' is a one-line reason, naming its class, why the implementations are known to canonicalize the vector differently; such a vector passes CheckCanonicalizable in both and carries no expected output until a later admission rule removes the difference. The difference is usually one of bytes: both implementations return canonical N-Quads, and they differ. It may instead be one of outcome: one implementation's canonicalizer cannot process the document, so that implementation's Canonicalize returns its canonicalization-failure error (ErrCanonicalizationFailed in Go), which is not an admission error, while the other returns N-Quads. A vector naming a context that only dataset.contexts supplies canonicalizes only under the loader that includes it; under the vendored contexts alone both implementations fail it while loading that context, which is not an admission refusal. The marked vectors, by class, are these and no others. Relative proof types from undefined terms (json-gold keeps the relative-IRI rdf:type objects, jsonld.js drops them): 'verifiable presentation embedding one credential as an array element'. Hollow graph containers, a proof graph container holding nothing jsonld.js turns into a statement (json-gold keeps a proof statement pointing at an empty graph, jsonld.js drops it): 'hollow graph container: an empty proof object', 'hollow graph container: a proof holding only an empty proof', 'hollow graph container: a proof holding only a term the context does not define', 'hollow graph container: a proof holding only an id', 'hollow graph container: a proof that is an IRI string'. A space in an IRI (json-gold keeps the statement, jsonld.js drops it): 'IRI with a space: a credential id holding U+0020'. A backslash or double quote in an IRI (json-gold escapes it, rdf-canonize writes it raw): 'IRI escaping: a credential id holding a backslash', 'IRI escaping: a credential id holding a double quote'. http(s) IRIs json-gold judges invalid (json-gold drops the node, jsonld.js keeps it): 'http(s) IRI json-gold rejects: a credential id with an invalid percent-escape (https://e.x/a%zz)', 'http(s) IRI json-gold rejects: a credential id with an empty host (https:///a)', 'http(s) IRI json-gold rejects: a credential id of 2083 code points'; the id of 2082 code points is an ordinary accept vector, because both keep it. IRIs Go's url.Parse rejects (json-gold drops the statement, jsonld.js keeps it): 'url.Parse class: an issuer IRI with an invalid percent-escape in a non-http scheme (foo:/a%zz)', 'url.Parse class: an issuer IRI holding U+0001', 'url.Parse class: an issuer IRI with a non-numeric port (foo://a:b/)'. A plain string in a graph container (json-gold emits a proof statement pointing at an empty graph, jsonld.js emits none): 'string in a graph container: a proof that is a plain string'. A number or boolean in a graph container, a difference of outcome (Go returns ErrCanonicalizationFailed, TypeScript admits the document and drops the value): 'scalar in a graph container: a proof that is the number 5', 'scalar in a graph container: a proof that is true'. A mixed-suite envelope, which honest traffic produces: a presentation under the W3C credentials v1, FulfillmentQuoteEnvelope and Ed25519 2020 contexts embedding a credential whose proof type no loaded context defines, so it expands to a relative IRI (json-gold keeps it as an rdf:type object, jsonld.js drops it): 'mixed-suite envelope: an Ed25519Signature2020 presentation under the FulfillmentQuoteEnvelope context embedding a credential whose proof type EcdsaSecp256k1RecoverySignature2020 no loaded context defines'. The marker is not a skip: each implementation's tests restate the exact list of vectors named here and pin that implementation's own side of each under every loader of the tests, either its output's length and SHA-256 together with the lines that output contains or lacks, or its canonicalization-failure outcome, so a marker added to another vector, removed from a named one, or left in place once the implementations agree fails the tests; the fix for the last is to replace the marker with the now-shared expected output and remove the vector from this list. The number of marked vectors is expected only to go down: each is a recorded difference awaiting an admission rule or a library fix that removes it.
